background_notes.fact: The compact set Cwin⊂Xn=ℝ^n is contained in [-rho,rho]^n for some finite real rho>0.

grounds.reason: At center tau>0, N002 supplies a compact Cwin.
Xn is finite-dimensional Euclidean space with standard continuous coordinates.

background_notes.justification: Each coordinate projection maps Cwin to a compact real set. Such a set is bounded: the increasing open intervals (-k,k), k positive integer, cover it, and a finite subcover supplies a finite bound. Taking a maximum over the finitely many coordinate bounds and increasing it by 1 gives rho>0. Empty Cwin or zero coordinates allow rho=1.

background_notes.fact: Lwin×Qbox is compact and there exists beta≥0 with |Dpar(r)(x)|≤beta for all r∈Lwin and x∈Qbox.

grounds.reason: F002 supplies rho>0 with Cwin contained in its coordinate cube.

background_notes.justification: Closed finite real intervals are compact and finite products of compact intervals are compact in the standard Euclidean topology, including the empty coordinate product. Thus Lwin×Qbox is compact. Composition with real absolute value is continuous. The preimages of (-k,k) under this continuous function cover the compact domain; a finite subcover bounds its absolute value by one finite positive integer, which supplies a nonnegative beta. An empty domain allows beta=0.

background_notes.fact: For finite rho>0 and beta≥0, Qbox=[-rho,rho]^n is Lebesgue measurable of measure (2rho)^n and bdom=beta·1_Qbox is integrable, with ∫|bdom| dx=beta(2rho)^n.

grounds.reason: The coordinates are standard orthonormal Euclidean coordinates.
dx is standard Euclidean Lebesgue measure.
The selected rho is a positive real number.
F003 supplies a finite nonnegative real beta.
bdom is the indicated piecewise constant function on Qbox.

background_notes.justification: The cube is a closed coordinate rectangle, hence Borel measurable. Standard Lebesgue measure assigns a coordinate rectangle the product of its side lengths, here (2rho)^n, finite. The nonnegative simple function beta·1_Qbox has integral beta times this measure; its absolute value equals itself, proving absolute integrability. For n=0 the product and the measure of the singleton Euclidean space are 1, so the same formula holds.
